docs.node.component: A node is the smallest thing the kit knows about: an `id` and a place among other nodes.
A bare node is already valid — it is not abstract and not a stub. Everything else a node can
do arrives as an atom: a small interface with its own fields, methods and events, composed in
at construction. There is no base class and no kind field, so behaviour asks for the atom it
needs rather than for a category.
```ts
import { node, mount } from "game-kit"
const root = node("root")   // a name and a place in the tree
mount(document.querySelector("#app"), root)   // nothing on screen yet
## Naming
You give a node its id; the node never invents one. The same node is read from several
places — another player's device, a save reopened tomorrow, a mock watching the same canvas —
and a counter hidden inside `node()` would be unique in one tab and nowhere else. When those
ids disagree, a move does not fail: it lands on a different existing node.
So ids come from outside the node, and there are two sources:
- **the spec**, for authored nodes — `board`, `hand`, `discard`. These are data, and every
device that loads the board reads the same ones.
- **the world's orchestrator**, for nodes that appear during play — the room, the save, or
`localIds()` when the instance answers to nobody.
Ids are opaque: nothing in the kit parses one, splits it or compares it to a literal. A
readable name is for you, not for the code.
## What `mount` does
`mount` is the host. It takes a DOM element to live in, creates the `view` inside it (an
`HTMLCanvasElement`), measures the viewport and watches it for resizes. Nodes are measured in
units; the host is the only part that knows what a unit is worth in pixels.
## Not everything is a node
A slot is an address, a spreading gap is a layout phantom, a shadow is a layer, a camera is a
way of looking — none of them has an id. Nor does a transaction, which sits above nodes and
moves them; asking one for its `z` or its shadow has no meaning.
